comparator.route: Economic History focus area with minor and internship
comparator.sourceNotes: The formal 2026-2027 ESHCC Teaching and Examination Regulations identify International Bachelor History as the English-language track of the History degree and establish the complete 180-EC structure, course names, credit weights, four focus areas and year-three options. The current programme pages corroborate the programme's English-language, global and social-science orientation and describe the focus areas and course content. Some public-page course labels are older descriptive names, so the exact 2026-2027 names and credits follow the TER. The generic target does not select a focus area or year-three option; Economic History and the minor/public-role/internship route are chosen by the neutral official-order tie-break, independently of UCR fit.

comparatorRouteSelection.route: Economic History focus area with minor and internship
comparatorRouteSelection.basis: The normalized International Bachelor History target does not select among four formally equal focus areas or the year-three options. The official 2026-2027 programme overview lists Economic History first, lists the minor/public-role/internship-or-electives option before exchange or the educational minor, and lists the internship before its two-elective substitute. These choices therefore follow official order before and independently of UCR course selection.

progressionAssessment.rationale: Modern History, introductory economics and sociology establish the historical, economic and social foundations in semester 1. Research Methods & Statistics precedes every selected economics course that formally requires it. Survey and thematic History courses lead to Native American Histories and the final History Research Seminar. Qualitative methodology, modern sociology and comparative politics precede advanced social theory, political philosophy and organisational analysis conceptually. The last three semesters integrate advanced History, economics, econometrics, behaviour, institutions and public rhetoric. Every course is available in its assigned term and every formal prerequisite is completed in an earlier semester.

alternativeSelection.assessment: The closest match owns the generic modern and global history identity, historical research, present-day relevance and the selected comparator route's Economic History direction. International Relations and Social and Cultural History remain distinct target-specific directions supported by formal focus areas and programme-interest evidence. Both yield coherent, mechanically feasible UCR curricula that differ materially from the closest match and from each other, so the maximum of three alternatives is reached.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both survey modern political, economic and cultural change across a broad chronological and international frame; UCR begins in 1815 rather than 1500.
Both compare societies through global encounters and unequal power; UCR ranges across empires more broadly and is not confined to 1300-1800.
Both trace the institutions, technologies and crises shaping modern societies; UCR does so through the specific history of warfare.
Both analyse colonialism, identity, belonging and changing historical orders; UCR concentrates on Native American histories.
Both develop advanced focus-area research through supervised historical inquiry and a substantial paper; the comparator class specifically prepares its separate bachelor thesis.

The UCR History Research Seminar develops historical research at advanced level but is already aligned to the comparator's focus-area thesis class; UCR has no separate introductory Becoming a Historian course.
UCR courses repeatedly connect past and present, but there is no separate historiography-and-contemporary-relevance course matching Rethinking History.
UCR offers philosophy courses, but none of the scheduled courses is a dedicated philosophy-of-history course.
The comparator requires a 15-EC individual History thesis. None of the 24 scheduled UCR courses is a thesis, so UCR's optional independent-research element is displayed alongside it.
The comparator component is an open History elective, while UCR elective choice is distributed throughout each 180-EC pathway; no single scheduled course is asserted as its equivalent.
Both teach research design and statistical analysis; the comparator applies those methods specifically to historical data.
Both teach systematic qualitative collection and interpretation; the comparator specialises in historical sources and techniques such as discourse, narrative and oral-history analysis.
Both develop structured academic argument and writing; the comparator culminates in a 4,000-word historical paper.
Both connect academic skills, professional identity and engagement with societal partners; the comparator specifically frames these as the public role of historians.
The comparator's 15-EC minor is an open external-field choice. UCR breadth is distributed across the full liberal-arts curriculum, so no one scheduled course is treated as the minor.
The selected comparator route requires a 15-EC field-specific internship. None of the scheduled UCR courses is an internship or equivalent workplace placement.
Both analyse international economic relations, globalisation, trade and changing national economies; UCR is an economics rather than a History course.
Both examine organisations and their relationships with institutions and power; UCR focuses on contemporary organisational behaviour rather than historical multinational-state relations.
Both supply concepts for interpreting growth, firms, labour and macroeconomic change; UCR is foundational and not a historical case course on emerging economies.
Both examine the relation between economic institutions, public policy and inequality; UCR uses economic theory and evidence rather than historical comparison.
Both introduce sociological concepts and theories as tools for understanding societies; the comparator applies them explicitly in historical research.

notes.text: The Erasmus programme is a coherent History degree with eight first-year History and historiography courses, specialised focus-area courses, dedicated quantitative and qualitative historical methods, a philosophy-of-history course, supervised thesis preparation, a 15-EC individual History thesis and an internship or another structured year-three option. UCR offers six History courses and can build strong historical pathways with economics, politics, sociology, law, heritage, literature and media, but it does not reproduce that continuous disciplinary sequence or required History thesis. These are close or related liberal-arts responses rather than substitutes for a full History major.
